items.title: Your AI Agents Need A Chief Operating Officer, Too
items.content: By Rick Folgmann A landlord in California has 21 days after a resident moves out to return the security deposit or send an itemized list of deductions. Miss it in bad faith, and the penalty can reach twice the deposit. That deadline doesn’t care whether the letter was supposed to come from a person or a piece of software. Either way, someone will answer for it. I think about this a lot. At my company, Get Covered, we now run 16 AI agents across more than 3 million rental units. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to. Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered. Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years. Gartner, meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review. Here is what has worked for us, and what I would advise any decision-maker to focus on when it comes to scaling. Start with work that already has a rulebook The best early candidates for agents are tasks where the rules already exist somewhere outside anyone’s head: a statute, a contract clause, an insurance requirement in a vendor agreement. Take vendor certificates of insurance. Across the industry, property teams spend roughly three hours per property every week chasing those documents by email. The work is tedious, however at the same time, it is completely specified. Assignments like these give decision-makers two advantages. First, the agent has something objective to check its output against, and second, your team can audit the result without debating judgment calls. items.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
items.content: Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the "preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications." Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft's hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.Read full article Comments

all_items.content: By Rick Folgmann A landlord in California has 21 days after a resident moves out to return the security deposit or send an itemized list of deductions. When we built them, the technical questions turned out to be the easier ones. The harder question, for each agent, was actually who it reports to. Rick Folgmann, COO at Get Covered. Most companies are about to face that same question, and few are ready for it. Deloitte’s 2026 State of AI survey found that 23% of companies use agentic AI at least moderately today, and 74% expect to within two years. Gartner, meanwhile, has predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Those numbers make a case for running agents the way you would run staff in a regulated job, with written rules, a defined scope, a manager and a regular review. all_items.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
all_items.content: Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II, an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the "preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications." Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft's hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot, which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot.
